pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You add a function to a package and want `go test` to run it as a test. What three things does the convention require, and what happens if you name it `Testlongest`?
expected_points: it must live in a file ending in _test.go, in the same package
the name must be Test followed by a non-lowercase letter, and it takes exactly one parameter, t *testing.T
Testlongest is silently skipped — go test still reports ok, so go test -v is how you confirm a test actually ran

questions.prompt: What is a table-driven test, and why does Go favor the pattern over writing one test function per input?
expected_points: cases live as data in a slice of (often anonymous) structs; one loop holds the checking logic
adding a case costs one line of data, so edge cases actually get added
the checking logic and failure message exist once, and the table reads as a specification

questions.prompt: What does wrapping each table case in t.Run buy you over a bare loop, and how do you run just the case named "empty slice" in TestAverage?
expected_points: failures name the exact case (TestAverage/empty_slice) instead of pointing at the whole loop
cases are isolated — t.Fatalf stops only that subtest, the loop continues
go test -run 'TestAverage/empty_slice' — slash separates function pattern from subtest pattern, spaces become underscores

questions.prompt: Your package shows 100% coverage from `go test -cover`. What does that number guarantee, and what does it not?
expected_points: guarantees every statement was executed by some test
does not guarantee outputs were checked or cases were well chosen — executed is not verified
the exercise proved it: the buggy Average line was fully covered by an evenly-dividing case and still wrong

questions.prompt: When do you reach for t.Fatalf instead of t.Errorf? Use your TestAverage as the example.
expected_points: Errorf marks failure and continues, letting one run report several mismatches
Fatalf stops the (sub)test immediately — right when continuing is meaningless, like getting an error where a value was needed
inside t.Run a Fatalf only kills that case, so the rest of the table still runs

questions.prompt: Why did Average([]int{2, 4}) hide the bug that Average([]int{1, 2}) exposed, and what general lesson about choosing test inputs follows?
expected_points: the bug was integer division truncating before the float64 conversion, invisible when the sum divides evenly
6/2 gives the right answer even when truncated; 3/2 does not
pick inputs where correct and plausibly-wrong implementations disagree — empty inputs, ties, uneven divisions, error paths
